core_idea: Relationships are a resource. For Bourdieu, social capital is the resources a person can draw on through membership in a durable network; it can be converted into economic and cultural capital and helps reproduce class inequality. Coleman and Putnam later framed it as the trust, norms and networks that make cooperation and collective action easier.
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: How do networks, trust or connections shape access to jobs, credit, education or power?
Why do some communities or organizations cooperate better than others?
Typical data: interviews on networks and help-seeking, network surveys, community case studies.
common_mistakes: Mixing Bourdieu (inequality, individuals and classes) with Putnam (communities, civic life) without saying which version you use.
Assuming more social capital is always good.
Measuring it with one proxy (e.g. number of memberships) and calling that social capital.
